Biointermediates for coprocessing in existing petroleum refineries Beyond the stringent regulatory requirements to achieve flight certification, many SAF pathways must also navigate complex societal issues involving the use of bio-feedstocks and arable farmland. This tension has become known as the “food versus fuel” debate. Although the environmental benefits and decarbonization potential of biofuels are well established, using edible feedstocks such as corn, sugarcane, virgin vegetable oils, etc. for fuel which could otherwise be used for food purposes inevitably leads to scrutiny around impacts on global food insecurity. Consequently, the SAF industry is actively seeking alternatives that avoid direct competition with food-grade feedstocks, instead favoring “second-” and “third-generation” feedstocks (e.g., cellulosic and aquatic biomass) that utilize inedible forms of biomass and/or marginal quality land. Moving forward, as these bio-based pathways seek to significantly ramp up production, sourcing feedstock while navigating the challenging while considering the issues around the food versus fuel debate and the associated land-use impacts will be a key issue for some SAF pathways as discussed in more detail below. 2.1.1 ASTM-Certified SAF Production Technologies 2.1.1.1 Fischer-Tropsch Synthetic Paraffinic Kerosene The first SAF pathway to become flight-certified was the FT pathway in 2009. Denoted as Annex 1, FT generates a product known as synthesized paraffinic kerosene (SPK), predominantly comprising isoparaffins and straight-chain paraffins (e.g., n-alkanes, iso-alkanes; see Figure 3). The FT pathway is a technically mature pathway of technology readiness level (TRL) 9 that has been utilized to produce fuels for more than century, originating in Germany during World War I.
